title: Roughly what would this system cost to run per month?
summary: A senior-signal question — tests whether you can translate compute, storage, and bandwidth estimates into a dollar figure, showing cost-awareness, not just capacity math.

slides.markdown:
"Roughly what would this system cost to run per month?" gets asked specifically at senior and staff levels, because it tests something capacity math alone doesn't: whether you connect an architecture to its dollar cost, and whether you'd flag an expensive design choice before it ships rather than after the first bill arrives.

The strong answer sums a few cost lines separately — compute, storage, bandwidth, managed-service premiums — and lands on an order-of-magnitude figure, not a spreadsheet-precise one.

Ask two things before pricing anything: **which cloud provider** are we assuming — pricing varies enough between AWS, GCP, and Azure that stating one avoids arguing over the wrong numbers — and **is this steady-state cost, or does it include the peak/spike capacity** from the earlier estimates?

Most of the time the honest answer is "steady-state, with a note that peak provisioning adds more" — say that explicitly rather than silently picking one.

The formula: **cost = compute + storage + bandwidth + managed-service premium**, summed as **separate line items**, not one blended guess. Each line reuses a number you likely already estimated earlier in the interview — server count, storage in GB, egress in GB — multiplied by a rough per-unit price.

Saying the formula out loud before pricing anything shows the interviewer this is a repeatable method, the same discipline used for QPS and storage, just applied to dollars. See [cost-and-org-aware design](cost-and-org-aware-design) for how cost trades off against other design decisions.

Reusing the earlier estimate of 27 app-server instances, priced at roughly $0.20/instance-hour, running the full month (730 hours):

```
27 instances x 730 hours/month = 19,710 instance-hours
19,710 instance-hours x $0.20/hour ~= $3,942/month (compute)
```

That's the app tier alone. Every other tier — database, cache, load balancer — gets its own line, priced the same way: quantity × time × rate.

Add the other two lines, priced against rough public rates: 50TB of storage at $0.023/GB-month, and 200TB of monthly egress at $0.08/GB.

```
Storage: 50,000 GB x $0.023/GB-month ~= $1,150/month
Egress:  200,000 GB x $0.08/GB     ~= $16,000/month
```

Notice egress alone is roughly **4x the compute line** — a pattern that surprises most candidates the first time they actually run these numbers, and a big part of why this question gets asked.

A managed database or queue (RDS, managed Kafka, a hosted Redis) typically costs noticeably more per instance-hour than the equivalent self-hosted box — here, say $0.35/hour managed versus $0.20/hour self-hosted, for 4 database instances: 4 × 730 × $0.35 ≈ **$1,022/month**, a real premium over the raw compute rate.

That premium buys automated failover, backups, patching, and an on-call burden someone else carries — often still the right trade even at a visibly higher line-item cost. Name the premium explicitly rather than pricing a managed service as if it were plain compute.

**Self-hosting** the database tier is cheaper per instance-hour and gives full control over tuning, but it puts failover, backups, patch management, and 2am pages on your own team. **Managed services** cost visibly more per unit — often 50-75% more — but remove an entire operational burden, letting the team focus on the product instead of database internals.

Name both sides explicitly: for most teams past a very early stage, the managed premium is worth it — the alternative is quietly paying for it anyway, in engineer time instead of a cloud bill.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what's the single biggest lever to cut this in half?
slides.markdown:
Total: roughly $3,942 + $1,022 + $1,150 + $16,000 ≈ **$22,100/month**. Egress alone is about 72% of that bill — so the single biggest lever isn't shrinking compute or negotiating reserved pricing, it's **cutting egress**, typically with a CDN.

If a CDN absorbs 90% of egress (as in the earlier bandwidth estimate), that line drops from $16,000 to about $1,600 — pulling the total down to roughly $7,700/month, well past cutting the original bill in half. Naming egress as the lever, not compute, is the senior-level answer here.

"Reserved pricing could cut this 30-40% — when do you commit vs stay on-demand?" Reserved/committed-use discounts apply to **compute and managed-DB spend**, not egress — here that's $3,942 + $1,022 ≈ $4,964, so even a 35% discount only saves about $1,740/month, roughly 8% of the total bill, because egress dominates.

Commit to reserved pricing once load is stable and predictable — a 1- or 3-year term is a bad bet on a workload that might shrink or change shape. Stay on-demand while the system, or the team's confidence in its shape, is still new.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a precise-looking number instead of an order of magnitude
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** presenting "$21,847.32/month" signals rigor and confidence.

**Why it's wrong:** every input in this estimate — instance price, egress rate, storage rate — was itself a rough public figure, so false precision on the output just advertises that you don't understand your own error bars. It also invites the interviewer to poke holes in a number you can't actually defend to two decimal places.

**Correct model:** present a round figure with its order of magnitude — "roughly $20-25k/month" — and name which line dominates it.

Compressed script: "Compute for 27 instances runs about $3,900/month, a managed database adds roughly $1,000, storage another $1,150, and egress is the big one at about $16,000 — call it $22k a month total. Egress alone is 72% of that, so a CDN absorbing most of it is the single biggest lever, not reserved pricing, which only touches compute and the database."

Practice naming the dominant line item — that's the part of the answer that shows judgment, not just arithmetic.
